title: Danish cultural participation is age- and place-shaped differently across digital games, cinema, museums, and heritage
source_unit: Statistics Denmark Cultural Habits Survey, Q2 2026, StatBank tables KV2HOVED and KV2URB
geography: Denmark; population cultural and recreational activity participation by age and degree of urbanisation

observations.period: Q2 2026; cultural and recreational participation within the previous 12 months by age

denominator.unit: persons drawn in each quarterly Statistics Denmark Cultural Habits Survey sample; published percentages are population estimates

digital_games_total.unit: percent participating in digital games within the previous 12 months

museum_total.unit: percent visiting a museum within the previous 12 months

cinema_age_gap.unit: percentage-point difference: cinema participation was 88% at ages 16-24 versus 48% at ages 75+

mechanism.value: Age is not a single cultural-participation gradient: digital games and cinema are sharply youth-skewed, while museum participation is comparatively age-flat, implying different access, routine, technology, and meaning pathways

observations.method: Descriptive extraction from Statistics Denmark StatBank table KV2HOVED for Q2 2026; percentages indicate people participating at least once in the previous 12 months, by activity and age.
observations.uncertainty: The survey uses four questionnaire versions and the questionnaire was changed from 2024, so results are not directly comparable with earlier versions. These are annual-recall, cross-sectional percentages, not frequency, intensity, spending, quality, or causal age effects.
observations.subgroup: Danish residents represented by the Cultural Habits Survey, by age group.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age differences may combine life stage, household composition, technology access, health, transport, education, social norms, and recall; museum parity does not establish equal affordability or welcome.

observations.period: Q2 2026; selected cultural participation by degree of urbanisation

denominator.unit: persons drawn in each quarterly Statistics Denmark Cultural Habits Survey sample; urbanisation percentages are population estimates

museum_dense_vs_thin.value: 71% densely populated areas versus 58% thinly populated areas
museum_dense_vs_thin.unit: percent visiting a museum within the previous 12 months

cinema_dense_vs_thin.value: 76% densely populated areas versus 64% thinly populated areas
cinema_dense_vs_thin.unit: percent visiting a cinema within the previous 12 months

concert_dense_vs_thin.value: 69% densely populated areas versus 61% thinly populated areas
concert_dense_vs_thin.unit: percent attending a concert or music festival within the previous 12 months

heritage_dense_vs_thin.value: 70% densely populated areas versus 67% thinly populated areas
heritage_dense_vs_thin.unit: percent visiting Danish cultural heritage sites or objects within the previous 12 months

urban_selectivity.value: Contemporary venue participation shows larger dense-to-thin gaps than Danish heritage-site participation

mechanism.value: Place selectively shapes cultural access: venue-based cinema, museum, and concert participation likely depend more on proximity and transport than heritage participation, which may be distributed through local or dispersed sites

observations.method: Descriptive extraction from Statistics Denmark StatBank table KV2URB for Q2 2026; urbanisation categories are densely populated, intermediate, and thinly populated areas.
observations.uncertainty: Urbanisation is an aggregate place classification, not a measure of venue supply, travel time, price, transport, household income, or individual mobility. The differences are descriptive and do not establish that urbanisation causes participation gaps.
observations.subgroup: Danish residents by degree of urbanisation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Dense-area differences may reflect age, education, income, tourism, population composition, cultural supply, or self-selection rather than a pure access effect; heritage-site parity does not mean equal experience or cultural belonging.
